topic: The 1961 Milgram obedience experiment and its unexpected outcome

script.title: The Milgram Experiment: Would You Actually Obey?
script.hook: Would you torture an innocent stranger if ordered to?

scenes.text: Would you torture an innocent stranger if ordered to?
In nineteen sixty-one, Yale researchers set up a chilling experiment.
Psychiatrists predicted less than three percent would deliver the maximum shock.

motion_action.statement: Psychiatrists estimated only 1 to 3% would administer the top shock

scenes.text: Roughly sixty-five percent of ordinary people went all the way.
They pressed the final button: four hundred and fifty deadly volts.

motion_action.statement: Participants were never physically forced or threatened

scenes.text: A calm man in a gray coat simply said: please continue.

motion_action.result_headline: The agentic state: surrendering personal responsibility

scenes.text: Authority quietly overrides our deepest moral instincts.
Which forces you to confront the darkest question:

script.loop_transition_text: Which forces you to confront the darkest question:
script.description:
The Milgram experiment revealed a terrifying truth about obedience to authority when tested under pressure.
Discover how ordinary participants delivered maximum shocks just because an experimenter told them to. Understand the psychology of compliance.

#Shorts #psychology #humanbehavior #mindset
script.comment_question: Honest answer: do you think you would have walked out, or pulled the switch?
sources: Milgram, S., 1963 (Behavioral Study of Obedience, JASP)
Milgram, S., 1974 (Obedience to Authority: An Experimental View)
review_notes: FIXED: Scene 3: "Compliance fell sharply after the first shocking shock." (In Milgram's experiment, 100% of participants complied past the initial shocks, with the first drop-off occurring only at 300 volts.)
